findings: The frozen artifact contract requires fit and retention of a nominal 170 x 170 mm Mini-ITX motherboard and accessible rear I/O.
The frozen PRD independently repeats a 170 x 170 mm Mini-ITX board envelope; this is a project compatibility requirement, not primary evidence for the published Mini-ITX mechanical standard.

Neither frozen input provides mounting-hole center coordinates, mounting-hole diameters or tolerances, motherboard thickness/component-height limits, or the rear-I/O chassis-aperture dimensions and datum relationship.

The frozen inputs do not name a motherboard model or revision, so connector bodies, connector centerlines, port stack geometry, socket/RAM/VRM locations, heatsinks, underside components, PCIe-latch access, cable bend envelopes, and local keepouts remain motherboard-model-specific rather than established standardized geometry.

The enclosure must expose motherboard rear I/O, but the available evidence does not establish whether CAD should use a conventional removable I/O-shield opening, an integrated motherboard I/O shield, or a model-specific rear-panel treatment.
recommendations: Treat only the nominal 170 x 170 mm envelope as a current project requirement; do not place standoffs or release enclosure CAD from an unverified internet mounting-hole sketch.

Before authoritative CAD is updated, obtain and archive the applicable published Mini-ITX mechanical specification/addendum plus the governing ATX chassis rear-I/O aperture drawing; record revision, drawing datum, units, tolerances, hole diameters, and aperture-to-board relationship.

Express any verified mounting pattern in a single explicit board coordinate frame, for example origin at the board corner formed by the rear-I/O edge and the adjacent side edge, with +X and +Y directions stated; do not silently transpose coordinates from drawings that use another view or datum.

After the user locks the motherboard, obtain its manufacturer mechanical drawing or measure the physical board and separately model its rear-I/O shield, connector protrusions, tall-component envelopes, underside keepouts, PCIe slot/riser access, and cable bend space.
Use the final motherboard or supplied I/O shield as the fit-check authority for model-specific rear-I/O geometry even after the standard chassis aperture is verified.

unresolved_decisions.question: Which exact Mini-ITX motherboard manufacturer, model, and hardware revision will be used?
unresolved_decisions.impact: This controls rear-I/O geometry, integrated-versus-separate shield treatment, connector and heatsink envelopes, underside keepouts, CPU/RAM locations, and cable clearances that the form-factor envelope alone cannot define.

unresolved_decisions.question: Should the enclosure support a conventional removable I/O shield, the locked motherboard's integrated I/O shield, or a motherboard-specific printed opening?
unresolved_decisions.impact: The choice changes rear-wall cutout geometry, retention features, insertion sequence, tolerance stack, and cross-motherboard compatibility.

warnings: No primary Mini-ITX/ATX mechanical-standard document or motherboard manufacturer mechanical drawing was available in the frozen evidence. Exact mounting-hole coordinates, hole diameters, rear-I/O aperture dimensions, offsets, and tolerances therefore remain unverified and are intentionally not invented in this report.

The phrase 'standard Mini-ITX' in project requirements is insufficient design authority for detailed enclosure features; nominal board size does not prove standoff placement or model-specific component clearance.
Do not confuse the standardized chassis I/O aperture, once verified, with the motherboard-specific connector cutouts and keepouts embodied by a separate or integrated I/O shield.
